introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Economics 2 (0725), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2023. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FIVE questions, choosing AT LEAST TWO from each section. All questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

figures.legende: Normal downward-sloping demand curve: a fall in price from P1 to P2 raises quantity demanded from Q1 to Q2 through the substitution and income effects (model answer to Q2(a)).

questions.enonce_markdown:
Using the income and substitution effects, explain the shape of a normal demand curve.

(10 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** A normal demand curve **slopes downward**: when the price of a good falls (other things equal), the quantity demanded rises. Economists explain this shape by splitting the effect of a price change into two parts: the substitution effect and the income effect.

![fig-1](gce-al-economics-2023-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_2_fig_1.png)

**1. The substitution effect.** When the price of a good falls, it becomes **relatively cheaper than its substitutes**. Rational consumers switch from the now relatively dearer goods towards the cheaper good, so the quantity demanded rises. *Example:* if the price of rice falls while the price of cassava and bread stays the same, households replace some cassava and bread by rice. The substitution effect always works in the same direction: a fall in price raises quantity demanded.

**2. The income effect.** A fall in the price of a good raises the **real income (purchasing power)** of consumers, although their money income has not changed: the same money now buys more. *Example (hypothetical):* a household spends 10 000 FCFA a week on rice at 500 FCFA per kg and buys $10\,000 / 500 = 20$ kg. If the price falls to 400 FCFA per kg, the same 20 kg costs only $20 \times 400 = 8\,000$ FCFA, so the household is in effect 2 000 FCFA richer, or it can buy $10\,000 / 400 = 25$ kg. With a higher real income, the consumer buys **more of a normal good** (a good whose demand rises with income), and the quantity demanded of it rises again.

**3. Combined effect and the shape of the curve.** For a **normal good**, both effects push in the **same direction**: a fall in price increases quantity demanded through substitution and through the rise in real income. The total effect is therefore an increase in quantity demanded as price falls, and the demand curve slopes **downward** from left to right (a movement from $P_1, Q_1$ to $P_2, Q_2$ in the diagram). The reverse happens when price rises.

**4. Other types of good (to qualify the answer).**
- **Inferior good** (for example cheap cassava flour or second-hand clothes): the substitution effect still raises demand, but the income effect works the other way, since a higher real income makes people buy *less* of it. As the substitution effect is normally stronger, the curve still slopes downward, but more steeply.
- **Giffen good**: if the negative income effect is **stronger** than the substitution effect, a fall in price reduces quantity demanded and the curve slopes **upward**. This is a rare exception.

**Conclusion.** The downward slope of a normal demand curve is explained by the substitution effect and the income effect working together.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Bring out the likely factors that will lead to an increase in the supply of a good.

(10 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The supply of a good is the quantity producers are willing and able to offer at each price in a given period. A change in the good's *own price* causes a movement along the supply curve (change in quantity supplied). An **increase in supply** means a **shift of the whole supply curve to the right**: more is offered at every price. It results from changes in the **conditions of supply**, namely:

1. **A fall in the cost of production** (wages, raw materials, rent, energy, interest on loans). Cheaper inputs raise profit per unit at each price, so firms offer more. *Example:* cheaper fertiliser or electricity raises the supply of maize or of processed cocoa.
2. **Improved technology and productivity.** New machinery, improved seeds, better farming methods, or training of workers lower unit costs and increase output at each price.
3. **Government subsidies and lower taxes.** A subsidy to producers (for example on fertiliser) reduces costs; a cut in production taxes or customs duties on inputs has the same effect. A higher tax would reduce supply.
4. **Favourable natural conditions.** Good rainfall and the absence of pests or floods raise agricultural supply (cocoa, coffee, cotton, plantain).
5. **An increase in the number of firms** (new entrants or expansion of existing firms), encouraged by profitable conditions, easier licensing or a better business environment.
6. **Changes in the prices of other goods.** A fall in the price of a good the firm could produce instead (a good in competitive supply) makes the firm shift resources to this good; a rise in the price of a good in joint supply (for example beef and hides) raises the supply of its by-product.
7. **Producers' expectations.** If producers expect the price to fall in the future, they may sell more now, so current supply increases; if they expect a rise, they may withhold stock and supply falls.
8. **Better infrastructure and a stable environment.** Better roads, electricity and transport reduce costs and losses (for example food perishing on the way to the market), and peace and political stability encourage production.
9. **Less restrictive regulation** or the lifting of import controls on inputs.
10. **Aims of the producers.** For instance, a firm that moves from profit-making to sales maximisation will offer more at each price.

**Conclusion.** Any of these changes shifts the supply curve to the right ($S_0$ to $S_1$): at the same price producers will supply more, and in the absence of a change in demand the market price falls and the quantity traded rises.
